Lockheed’s Skunk Works plans to build four more of its multirole combat drones
The firm’s top secret research arm shared new Vectis images, but few key details.
Skunk Works, Lockheed Martin’s secretive research arm, plans to build four more of its experimental, multipurpose drones as the firm attempts to sell its futuristic platform to the U.S. military.
Last year, Skunk Works unveiled Vectis—a concept for a group 5 drone that’s capable of a wide range of missions. Now, on the first day of the Air & Space Force Association’s defense conference near Washington, D.C., company officials announced they’re making significant progress on the prototype and are already planning to expand the fleet for more tests.
“We are moving forward with a plan to build an additional four vehicles, bringing a total of five to include the original prototype,” said Ron Fehlen, Skunk Works’ vice president and general manager. “Development work on those additional aircraft is already underway, and we'll have more specifics to share soon.”
Company officials shared new images of the Skunk Works combat drone with reporters ahead of this week’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference. Vectis will be roughly 34 feet long and have a 38-foot wingspan, and will feature a submerged engine inlet and a tail-less body to reduce drag and mission flexibility,” Fehlen said. While Lockheed was eager to talk about the aircraft’s design, the Skunk Works vice president was tight-lipped about who the specific customer for the new aircraft could be, and didn’t provide details on the weapons loadout, propulsion system, or estimated cost of the platform. The Air Force, Marine Corps, and Navy are all aiming to field collaborative combat aircraft.
“From an affordability standpoint, which we're always looking at, and, of course, are targeting to be the CCA competitive price. So we're very cognizant of it and make trades associated with that, Fehlen said. “It's obviously, I think, focused more on the CCA side of the house, and obviously the price points that are highly relevant in that regime.”
Fehlen said the company remains on track to fly Vectis by “the end of 2027.” He said Skunk Works feels confident in that timeline, due in part, to the use of digital designs and “minimal tooling determinant assembly”—which the Skunk Works vice president likened to ready-to-assemble furniture with pre-drilled holes.
“It's a technique that really enables an increased level of affordability and speed through really reducing the amount of touch labor required and increasing the first pass yield,” Fehlen said. “We've seen in many cases an 80 percent reduction in labor hours to build up the aircraft itself.”
While Fehlen wouldn’t specify one specific U.S. program or customer Vectis is geared toward, he did say it could work with any of Lockheed Martin’s fighter jets, which are also flown by other nation’s militaries.
“I'll point to the fact that we have a long history in crewed tactical systems that, you know, Vectus is going to need to integrate with, in addition to other fighter aircraft that are produced around the world,” Fehlen said. “So, from our perspective, this is in line with our heritage and what we're producing today and delivering to the field. It has incredible capability, and now we're going to be able to add this to it.”

b89db9283116.text: President Trump is as all-in on AI as a politician could be: all gas, no brakes, and zero interest in hand-wringing about dystopian risks or public disdain. Democrats are as conflicted on AI as a party could be: skeptical of the labs, spooked by their warnings, but split on whether to shut it all down. Why it matters: This staggering divide makes consensus on federal AI regulation almost unimaginable this year — and probably through early 2029, regardless of who wins control of Congress. Zoom in: Trump has governed as the AI president from Day 1 , applying the same doctrine to models and the data centers that power them — build faster, regulate less, beat China. Speaking in Ireland on Sunday, he dismissed new safety warnings as the work of "a lot of negative forces ... bringing up things that won't happen" — and reduced the stakes to one line: "Whoever wins AI wins." It's unclear which "negative forces" Trump has in mind: Calls to slow the race — or " pace the frontier " — are now coming from the leaders of America's premier AI labs, including Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google. Between the lines: Trump's accelerationist allies, including venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, see the safety alarms as a cynical ploy by the field's dominant players to lock in favorable regulations. David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar and a leading voice for the administration's hands-off approach, has a simple answer : Slow yourselves down. If OpenAI and Anthropic truly think the frontier is moving too fast, Sacks argues, they can decelerate on their own without using Washington to force competitors to do the same. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) echoed Sacks' argument that the labs don't need Congress to slow themselves down — and rejected calls for an emergency moratorium. Johnson said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he'd recall the House and put AI regulation to a vote "if we had the solution," but warned Congress against rushing into rules it doesn't yet understand. His preferred first step is a summit: Johnson said Sunday he wants Trump, congressional leaders and the heads of the major AI labs in a room as soon as possible to hammer out a common approach to safety. The other side: Congressional Democrats are coalescing around urgency, but have no comparable doctrine on what to actually do. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says his caucus will meet Tuesday to debate what action to take, while former President Barack Obama is privately urging the party to make AI a top priority. The policy spectrum is vast — and doesn't neatly map onto what the labs themselves are asking for. On the progressive end, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) want to ban superintelligence outright, pause advanced AI development and threaten violators with up to 20 years in prison . Others are reaching for more conventional Washington fixes: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) wants a bipartisan AI select committee with subpoena power, while Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is demanding that OpenAI open its models to federal safety reviews. What to watch: The unprecedented push for restraint from inside the AI industry, colliding with deepening public unease, could scramble this political stalemate. Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers, a Trump ally running in a swing state, said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's new warning convinced him "we must slow down development" so government can catch up. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) is investigating AI's "existential risk," while Sens. John Thune (R-S.D.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) are pursuing a narrower plan requiring companies to test and report catastrophic risks. Reality check: Political pressure and lobbying could crack open the door to narrow bipartisan measures, though any meaningful regulation would still have to survive Trump's veto pen. The bottom line: Washington is deeply divided on whether AI is a national triumph to unleash or a national emergency to contain.

At a moment when the US is reconsidering the extent and purpose of its engagement abroad, I find myself returning to a lesson I confronted often in my time in government: After more than five decades working on Africa, one of the most important things the US can do is show up and listen.
The story of how the African Growth and Opportunity Act came together in 1999 is instructive as I recall in my memoir. We were preparing to roll out AGOA under the Clinton administration and invited the leadership of the African diplomatic corps to the State Department for a briefing. We told the ambassadors that only 10 countries would be selected and that their governments would be informed through our ambassadors in Africa.
That went over like a lead balloon.
The dean of the group, the highly respected Roble Olhaye of Djibouti, reminded us that the diplomatic corps had been advocating for AGOA for five years. They had been updating their capitals and lobbying Congress for the legislation. How, he asked, could we treat them in such a âshabby manner?â
He was right. We had not been listening.
So we changed course, inviting more than 180 ministers from 43 African countries to Washington for four days of discussions with President Bill Clinton, cabinet members, Congress, business leaders, and civil society representatives to discuss trade, investment, conflict prevention, food security, democracy, and human rights.
We then went back to the list of potential AGOA beneficiaries and determined that 32 African countries met the conditions of the legislation.
The rest, as they say, is history.
More than a quarter-century later, AGOA is again in flux. Congress extended the program through the end of 2026, and the Trump administration has said it wants to modernize the legislation to align with its America First trade policy and create more opportunities for US businesses.
This creates an opportunity to ask a bigger question: What should the US-Africa commercial relationship look like for the next 25 years?
The answer should not be developed in Washington alone.
Africa has changed dramatically since AGOA was created. It is building a continent-wide market, while its governments are seeking investment in manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, and technology, while looking to add value to their mineral resources.
The US has interests of its own: new markets for American companies, resilient supply chains, and access to critical minerals. Those interests can align with African priorities, but Washington should not assume they do.
That is why listening is a strategic tool, not simply a diplomatic courtesy. If Washington wants American companies to compete more effectively in Africa, it first needs to understand what its potential partners actually want.
That is why the Trump administration should convene the US-Africa Ministerial called for in the recently extended AGOA legislation â and make the meeting more than a ceremonial gathering. It should bring together African governments, continent-wide blocs such as the African Union, US and African businesses, investors, and civil society to help shape the next generation of the relationship.
The goal should be more than modernizing a trade preference program. It should be to identify where US and African interests genuinely intersect â and where they do not â and build policy around that reality.
There is a broader lesson here for US policy toward Africa. A relationship centered more heavily on trade, investment, and mutually beneficial commercial opportunities can be entirely consistent with Americaâs interests.
But transactional does not have to mean transactional-only.
The most successful commercial relationships are built on knowledge, trust, and sustained engagement. My experience in 1999 taught me that showing up is not enough. You have to listen before you decide what the partnership should look like.
That is as true for the next 25 years as it was for the first 25.
Witney W. Schneidman is the author of This Africa Idea: A Memoir of Discovery, Diplomacy, and Opportunity, published by Bloomsbury. He served as the Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Africa during the Clinton Administration.

The News
Uber was paying Nigerian drivers more than it charged passengers for some short trips, an unsustainable subsidy that played a leading role in the US ride-hailing giantâs abrupt exit this month, according to a new report based on thousands of Uber trips.
The company quit Nigeria and Uganda on Sept. 2, the same day it announced a global restructuring decision that cut 10% of its staff globally. It still operates in four African countries including South Africa and Kenya.
Even after 12 years of operating in Nigeria, Uber did not have a large enough number of active passengers there and high inflation and currency depreciation made passengers increasingly price sensitive, according to a report by Obi, a California-based price and trip data aggregator that tracks more than half-dozen ride hailing platforms.
âItâs obvious that demand [in Nigeria] was low and that the political and economic climate wasnât helping,â Ashwini Anburajan, CEO of Obi, told Semafor. âPay had to be subsidized to make drivers willing to take rides. There was just no way for Uber to dig itself out of this pattern,â Anburajan said.
Her firmâs data suggests that Uber paid Nigerian drivers more than it charged passengers on trips shorter than 12 miles (20 km). In some cases, the company paid drivers 23% more than the passenger was actually charged. Though the company adjusted this pattern above the 12-mile threshold, it amounted to an âover-generousâ subsidy scheme for short rides that drivers would not have otherwise accepted, an approach that Uberâs in-country rivals like InDrive did not resort to, Obi said.
A typical Uber driver in Nigeria averaged 130 rides over the first seven months of 2026, but that was just over a tenth of the volume of rides the companyâs drivers in South Africa fulfilled over the same period, the report first shared with Semafor showed. Yet, Nigerian drivers kept a larger share of the fare paid by passengers compared to their counterparts in South Africa, the firm said. Its report is based on data from more than 20,000 rides completed by more than 300 drivers within the period on Uber and InDrive, a Russian-founded US company that also operates in Nigeria.
Step Back
Uberâs arrival in Nigeria in 2014 heralded a taxi revolution after a couple handful of startups attempted ride-hailing services in Lagos with little success. The company rode in aggressively with more than a billion dollars in investor capital to upstage the cityâs often rickety yellow cabs, promising technology-aided transport efficiency to passengers and dependable income to drivers.
This monthâs decision to pull out came after several attempts to stay relevant, from floating courier services and boat taxis, to multiple fare rises implemented to reflect higher costs of doing business following economic policy changes that have been rolled out since 2023.
Fuel prices have risen more than five-fold in Nigeria since the end of a government fuel subsidy scheme, and the naira currency has depreciated by more than 70% in that period, a combination that depresses net incomes both for drivers and transport companies. Some Nigeria analysts have cited a âchallenging macroeconomic environmentâ as the root cause of Uberâs exit as more expensive taxis became less preferred to relatively cheaper alternatives like buses, tricycles and motorcycles.
Know More
InDrive and Estonian company Bolt were Uberâs main Nigeria competitors and are now the main beneficiaries of the latterâs exit. Their ability to tweak parts of their operations to local sensibilities â like InDriveâs bargaining feature, and Boltâs flexibility with trip cancellation, car models and payment options â diminished the advantages Uber had gained from a two-year headstart, some analysts have argued.
Bolt, which pushed into offering three-wheeled taxis outside of Lagos, had won 60% of Nigeria market share by the time of Uberâs exit, Obi said. Active Nigerian users reached 3.3 million last December, more than six times that of Uber, according to Sensor Tower, a California-based app usage tracker.
Anburajan agrees with the view that localization may have helped Uber. âKeeping your business model and experience for users and drivers relatively uniform across markets can work if your target riders are international travelers who will place value on an experience thatâs the same from one country to the next,â she said. Ride-hailing will remain compelling and competitive in Africa for companies with âan approach that works for locals,â she said.
Ultimately, though, size does not equal a large opportunity. The upshot of Obiâs report is that there is simply no scale for Uber to absorb losses that must inevitably result from âa bad combinationâ of low per-driver volume and a per-ride subsidy. âA platform that has to raise prices by 71% and still needs to subsidize a large share of its rides is in a structural hole it canât price its way out of.â
Room for Disagreement
Some analysis of Uberâs exit blames the company for undercutting Nigerian drivers through unilateral fare cuts, prompting the drivers to revolt and port to rivals like Bolt.
On the other hand, the exit may be due to a shift in long-term priorities. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said the 10% cut to the companyâs global staff was about âfocusing our people and investments against the biggest opportunities ahead of us.â That has been widely interpreted as reflecting Uberâs increasing shift towards self-driving taxis, evidenced by the companyâs rollout of 15 robotaxis in London after the headcount cut. It is a line of business that is not yet viable in most African cities due to under-developed road networks and other factors.
Notable
- Uberâs Nigeria exit and overall experience in Africa âundercuts the assumption that U.S. technology companies will inevitably dominate every market they enter,â Onyeka Aralu, a competition fellow at the International Center for Law & Economics in Oregon, argues.

a3cfcdb6206c.text: By — Alex Veiga, Associated Press Alex Veiga, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/what-to-know-about-recent-dire-ai-predictions-and-calls-for-safeguards Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about recent dire AI predictions and calls for safeguards Science Sep 14, 2026 8:09 AM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — New warnings from within the artificial intelligence industry have revived a long-running debate over whether advanced AI could escape human control and ultimately threaten humanity's survival, and whether the companies developing the technology are doing enough to prevent such a scenario. The CEO of Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind Claude, said he thought the industry needed to reduce the speed of its work, cautioning Saturday that a swarm of AI agents might be able to take over the internet in six months to a year unless companies devoted more time to putting safeguards in place. READ MORE: Anthropic CEO says AI industry needs to give safety measures time to catch up Dario Amodei outlined a plan for companies like his and governments around the world to ensure that increasingly capable AI models remain aligned with the commands and values of responsible people days after two former Anthropic safety researchers publicly aired concerns that the existential threats AI might pose to humanity were receiving too little attention. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Here's what to know about the recent dire predictions and whether any brakes might be put on AI advancement. AI models are becoming more powerful Concerns over the potential risks of the technology are rising as new AI models become more powerful, heightening both the potential for misuse by people with criminal aims, such as creating and spreading a disease that kills most of the world's population, and the risk of AI systems going rogue in a dangerous way. Anthropic disclosed last week that it blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI models for malicious activity, such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapons. WATCH: AI researcher warns companies are ignoring catastrophic risks The company said it put stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could be used to make weapons but noted that "as models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society's defenders act to make them safer." Last year, Anthropic reported that hackers used the company's AI in a cyberattack targeting about 30 companies and government agencies around the world. It said the hackers were very likely from a Chinese state-sponsored group. Multiple AI models have acted on their own When an AI agent "goes rogue," it means the AI has taken action beyond the task it was asked to perform. Danantara was founded in 2025 and values its holdings at about $1 trillion, making it about as big as Saudi Arabiaâs Public Investment Fund. Itâs a young learner trying to compress what Sjahrir calls the âwalk, run, sprintâ trajectory of more established government investment vehicles while avoiding their mistakes; Saudi Arabia lost billions trying to make a splash in Silicon Valley, while Malaysiaâs 1MDB collapsed in a corruption scandal. Graft and political influence are particular concerns among international investors whose goodwill Indonesia, which runs both a budget deficit and a trade deficit, needs.
Sjahrir, who comes from Jakarta by way of Andover and the University of Chicago, has a two-sided mandate: to restructure more than 1,000 state-owned enterprises â half of them unprofitable â into dividend payers that can eventually go public; and to invest internationally in ways that bring economic benefits, like jobs and export-bearing industries, not just financial returns, back to Indonesia. A recent deal will see Danantara take a slice of meatpacking giant JBSâ Australian business in exchange for JBS helping to build Indonesiaâs meat industry.
Danantara has hired Neuberger Berman to help select deals and managers, is preparing to make its first allocations to hedge funds later this year, and is sending some of its own executives to secondments with Wall Street firms, Sjahrir said.
âIâm trying to learn from all the other sovereigns,â Sjahrir said. When asked whether heâs worried about being seen by Wall Street as easy money, he says: âI cannot change what they think. My focus is: Can we deploy capital well, make good returns, and are they bringing something to the table for us? Perception shifts.â
Q&A
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Liz Hoffman: The power dynamic between sovereign wealth funds and Western partners is changing fast. How do you think about what youâre getting back for the money youâre handing to Wall Street?
Pandu Sjahrir: Iâm trying to learn from all the other sovereigns. Weâre the youngest. We just got so big so fast, and I realized you have to learn to walk, then run, then sprint.
What did you learn from the âwalkâ phase?
Thereâs a reason [global asset managers and companies] exist. They know what theyâre doing. So partner with them, but say, âif we become a customer or partner of yours, can you also bring some of that skill set back to our country?â Our country is large enough â 300 million people, fifth-largest in the world. It can also be an addressable market for you. Itâs a good trade.
One thing Western money managers want is access to financial markets that have been off-limits in the past. Is that something Indonesia is open to?
Yes. Americaâs greatest asset has been its public markets. This is one of the models all of us want to replicate. So weâve offered: Invest with us, name the valuation, come into our stock market â and then tell us how to change it to compete, to make it bigger. Weâre willing to offer something very good, because a stock market is a monopolistic business. The only thing we ask in return is: Can you help us improve it?
Weâve started deploying capital with selected fund managers. But in each one, we want partnership. Weâre also, in the second half of this year, sending some of our guys to train with these managers.
Whatâs in it for them to train your people?
In five years, these guys will be the best we have and most likely in director or managing director roles. Itâs up to the [private-equity firms] whether they want that future investment-committee member, the one who will be saying yes or no, to be in their corner. Itâs the cheapest investment a GP can make.
How do you keep them from seeing you as dumb money in the meantime?

That was a painful lesson for a lot of the Gulf sovereigns. They spent the 2010s throwing money around because Wall Street was making them feel special and they got little back strategically.
Thatâs why we do direct deals only where we have the expertise. If we do a nickel deal for downstream processing, weâre quite good at that. But if you tell me, Pandu, do a deal with an LLM company or a data center in Texas â I donât think weâre the right party for it.

Weâre doing a deal with CIC out of China â $1 billion to invest in general partners together, because access in China is restricted and I need someone who knows the landscape.
You went to school at UChicago. Thatâs a very specific type of economics education.
Very pure. My second year, I took [Nobel laureate] Gary Beckerâs class. He said to us: âIf you get an A-minus or above, youâll work under me. B-plus, youâll probably get your Chicago PhD. B, youâll be a professor at Yale, Harvard, or Stanford. C-plus, youâll most likely go into private equity or investment banking.â
And?
I got a C-plus.

Authorities in Zambia have warned people not to eat meat from wildlife after dozens of wild animals, including hippos, elephants, buffalo and a crocodile died following an anthrax outbreak.
A disaster management agency official said over the weekend that 12 people had been infected with the disease after consuming dead wildlife in the Munyamadzi River area.
The official urged the public not to consume meat from animals that die naturally or from unknown causes, while urging the public to report any such cases.
Authorities have also called for hunting in the affected area to be suspended until the extent of the disease and associated risks are established.
Officials have not yet ascertained the full geographical extent of the latest outbreak, with surveillance and laboratory investigations ongoing.
Anthrax is endemic to Zambia but human deaths are not common. In 2023, the country experienced what was described as an "unprecedented outbreak", which killed four people and spread to nine out of 10 provinces.
Another large-scale outbreak was reported in 2011, with more than 500 cases, when five people died after consuming meat from infected hippos.
In the latest outbreak in the Munyamadzi Game Management Area, in Muchinga province, Zambia's Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit said 46 hippos, eight elephants, five buffaloes and one crocodile had died since July.
"The sad story about the deaths of this wildlife is that the carcasses ended up being eaten by the local people - that's what they depend on for their food," said the unit's national coordinator Norman Chipakupaku.
No human deaths have been reported, and the 12 infected people are currently receiving treatment.
Anthrax is caused by a bacteria called Bacillus anthracis, which largely survives as spores that hide away in soil for years before entering an animal through inhalation or a cut or wound.
It mainly affects grazing animals and can lead to sudden death. It can be transmitted from animals to humans through contact with contaminated animal products.
Zambians have been urged not to consume, sell, distribute or handle meat from animals that have died suddenly or from suspected anthrax. The public has also been advised against handling wild animals.

China has hit out against what it has called "threat narratives" over AI governance and warned against "engaging in confrontation and malicious competition".
It follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development - but in a way that prevents China from pulling ahead in the AI race.
Over the past week, industry insiders at the leading US artificial intelligence labs have been warning in extremely stark terms about the potential threat AI poses, with some saying it could wipe out humanity.
But US President Donald Trump has said that his priority is making sure the US develops the tech faster than China.
On Monday, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters that "narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition serve only to disrupt the process of global AI governance and are not in anyone's interest".
"All parties should work together to advance AI in a manner that is open, inclusive, beneficial to all, and oriented toward the good," he added.
His comments highlight the difficulties in getting an agreement between the world's two leading AI powers.
An agreement between the US and China to regulate AI development is "next to impossible", says Chang Jun Yan, an assistant professor with the military studies programme at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
"As part of each state's core national security interests, cooperation in taking things slower and more safely in relation to AI, is very, very unlikely."
Artificial intelligence now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech. Despite US export bans on critical chips, Chinese AI innovation has been expanding, driven by open-source technology and Beijing's backing.
Many experts believe the US is still ahead, and Chinese firms are trying to catch up as they struggle to raise the hundreds of billions of dollars that investors are ploughing into American AI.
But Beijing, including Chinese leader Xi Jinping himself, has also spoken about the risks posed by AI. China must "balance development and security", and introduce and improve relevant laws and ethical guidelines, and strengthen prevention of risks, to "safeguard the interests of the people and national security", state security minister Chen Yixin wrote on Sunday.
He warned of the dangers of "hostile forces" such as foreign intelligence using AI and called for international cooperation.
"There are strong signals that Washington and Beijing share an understanding of frontier risks," Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote recently.
China has "technical reasons" to work with the US, she argues, because its developers would be able to see how their models are deployed outside China, and detect and understand vulnerabilities.
In July, China set up the World AI Cooperation Organisation, which aims to shape global AI governance. And speaking at the Brics summit in India on Sunday, Xi proposed creating a community for open-source AI.
All this comes as calls for AI regulation grow louder in the US, especially after a former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week that "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.
Since then top industry bosses, such as Dario Amodei, have called for a slowdown and more regulation.
"We need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities," Open AI's chief executive Sam Altman wrote on X on Monday, which was echoed by Microsoft boss Satya Nadella who said AI development "cannot be controlled by a handful of entities".
But US President Donald Trump downplayed the risks, saying that he wanted to keep the US's lead over China "because whoever wins AI, wins".
The competition is fierce.
The former Anthropic employee Coxon told the BBC that there needed to be "some sort of coordinated slowdown with China, if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale".
As Trump prepares to host Xi at the White House next week, the two sides are trying to include AI on the agenda, the South China Morning Post reports.
It is also likely to be part of the talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, who are trying to meet before next week's summit, the paper said. Vice-Premier He runs the agency that oversees the country's economic planning, including AI development.
While collaboration between the US and China is important, experts say the stakes are high for both countries.
"If China establishes a durable lead in frontier AI, this will not be viewed in Washington as losing a technology race," says Chasen Nevett, managing director at Hong Kong-based firm, Forani Investments.
"It will be viewed as losing part of the strategic infrastructure of the next industrial era."
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia

Musk's SpaceX company has launched thousands of Starlink satellites into orbit in order to provide internet services, including in remote and rural areas.
The council's pilot scheme, which has been developed alongside the Greater Lincolnshire Forum for Agriculture and Horticulture, aims to "develop potential solutions to rural connectivity".
Farmers who want to be involved in the trial are being asked to get in touch.
Once the infrastructure is in place on the ground, farmers would need to subscribe to Starlink to use the service.

Barely-there particles called neutrinos just got caught acting even more ethereal.
With tiny masses and no electric charge, the subatomic particles rarely interact with anything, making them difficult to detect. Scientists have now spotted neutrinos with lower energies than any they’ve seen before. And they did it using a detector meant for another purpose entirely.
XENONnT, at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso in Italy, is designed to search for dark matter, the mysterious substance that is needed to explain the behavior of galaxies across the universe. It has yet to find any — although a similar detector has seen a tantalizing hint. What it has found, instead, are neutrinos — hundreds of them, researchers report in a paper submitted August 29 to arXiv.org.
Neutrinos are born in vast numbers in the sun — about 100 billion of them pass through your thumbnail every second. Some of those solar neutrinos are expected to interact in XENONnT. So the researchers went neutrino hunting.
The team found evidence of neutrinos smacking into electrons within the detector, producing light that revealed their presence. It’s the first time a dark matter detector has spotted neutrinos based on their electron-jostling antics. The detection met a statistical benchmark of 5 sigma, which physicists typically consider the threshold for a definitive detection.
Other dark matter detectors have seen hints of this process. In July, PandaX-4T, at the China Jinping Underground Laboratory in Liangshan, saw evidence of low-energy neutrinos, but at a statistical significance of about 2.2 sigma — not enough to make the detection a sure thing.
The neutrinos have energies as low as 17 kiloelectron volts. That’s about a tenth the energy of the wimpiest neutrinos previously detected. The newfound low-energy neutrinos are produced in the main fusion reaction that powers the sun, in which two protons merge to form a larger atomic nucleus.
The particles could carry the sun’s secrets. With a proposed, more advanced detector, “we expect to be able to extract valuable knowledge about the sun’s composition,” says XENONnT physicist Florian Jörg of the University of Zurich.
In 2024, XENONnT saw higher energy neutrinos from the sun, as did PandaX-4T. Those neutrinos are by-products of a different, less predominant type of fusion reaction, making them less numerous, but easier to spot. Detectors can catch these higher-energy neutrinos interacting with an entire nucleus instead of just a single electron.
The signature of a low-energy neutrino bouncing off an electron is easily confused with hordes of other interactions that can mimic it, called background. “The difficulty is picking the neutrino needles out of the background haystack,” says neutrino physicist Kate Scholberg of Duke University, who was not involved with the study. The researchers “look to have done a pretty heroic job on this.”

A pack of African wild dogs has completed a record-breaking 2,485-mile (4000km) journey across the continent.
Scientists say it is the furthest recorded distance for any African land mammal searching for a mate, offering hope that wildlife can travel across vast distances despite growing human pressures.
The three brothers zigzagged across Zambia, navigating a landscape increasingly shaped by people and avoiding obstacles including major cities.
However, other wild dogs tracked with GPS collars in the study died in illegal snares, underlining the dangers they face.
Three sisters almost completed an equally epic journey, but stopped when one became trapped in a snare.
African wild dogs are among Africa's rarest predators, with only about 6,000 remaining in the wild.
They live in highly social packs, hunt together and are known for their vast roaming in search of new territory and breeding opportunities with other packs.
They cannot breed within the pack they are born into, so they either wait and may eventually inherit their pack, or set off at the age of two or three in search of a mate.
The brothers covered about 260 miles in a straight line over the course of eight months, but travelled nearly 10 times that overall while crossing through a broken-up landscape.
These sorts of journeys are known as dispersals - travelling one way in search of a mate, which is a behaviour distinct from migrations, where animals move back and forth with the seasons in search of food or habitat.
The UN Convention on Migratory Species identifies Africa's longest migrations as wildebeest moving seasonally between Tanzania and Kenya in search of grazing and water covering more than 400 miles.
Globally, caribou undertake the longest single land migrations of any animal - travelling 839 miles in a round trip, while grey wolves have been recorded travelling more than 4,350 miles over a year.
Perhaps even more significant than the distance itself was the route the wild dogs took through Zambia.
They moved between wildlife strongholds, skirting areas containing major human obstacles, including the capital, Lusaka, and heavily developed industrial areas.
The findings suggest wild dog populations across eastern and southern Africa may remain more connected than conservationists previously believed.
Professor Scott Creel of Montana State University, the paper's lead author, who has been studying African wild dogs since 1991, said the study provides cautious optimism.
"It's plausible to believe that every major wild dog population in eastern and southern Africa, other than fenced ones, are potentially connected," he said.
But he said, in conservation,"the glass is half empty and the glass is half full", highlighting the threat of poaching snares.
While the three male wild dogs successfully completed their extraordinary journey, two of the three females died.
Researchers identified a pattern in which surviving pack members repeatedly returned to the same location, a behaviour that often signals the death of a companion.
The research, published in the journal, Ecology, external, adds weight to calls to create strips of natural land outside protected areas that connect separate wildlife areas broken apart by roads, towns, or farms.
Bruce Ellender, one of the paper's co-authors and Kafue Conservation director for the environmental charity, The Nature Conservancy, said species that roam over large areas, such as wild dogs and elephants, need connected landscapes if they are to survive into the future.
"We can't see these protected areas as islands and expect them to be functional in the long term, we need to think much broader than that," he said.

In the deep, dark Australian Abyss, what’s visible can be scarier than the unseen. There, giant sea spiders with glowing 25-centimeter-long legs may scuttle like disembodied apparitions.
Photos of these creatures unambiguously confirm that they exhibit bioluminescence, researchers report in the October Deep Sea Research Part I: Oceanographic Research Papers.
“It’s quite impressive for people scared of spiders,” says Jérôme Mallefet, a marine biologist with the Catholic University of Louvain in Belgium.
Mallefet and his colleagues discovered this phenomenon on a 2017 expedition to survey part of the deep-sea trench off southeastern Australia. Working out of a makeshift darkroom aboard the RV Investigator, he tested any of the 25,000 specimens suspected of bioluminescence hauled up in nets from up to nearly 5,000 meters deep. Some 76 percent of deep-sea creatures produce their own light — and it’s a trait that dates to 540 million years ago.
“I spent most of my time in 6° Celsius, in a dark cold room,” Mallefet says. “I believe I was a little bit crazy, but I like that.”
Poking the biggest of these sea spiders(Colossendeis tasmanica) raised a dim light. But adding potassium chloride, which can excite bioluminescent cells, had them glowing for up to 10 minutes, Mallefet and his colleagues showed. Another giant sea spider, C. minor, also exhibited bioluminescence.
The images confirm sporadic descriptions of bioluminescence in sea spiders, including a particularly poetic one from more than a century ago: “The creature, as it lay on its back, shone like a star, all its legs being lit along their ventral surface with a strange blue radiance.”
Most of the glow is on the underside of their legs, where their digestive tract is located, Mallefet says. That suggests that these spiders might get their bioluminescent properties from creatures they eat like sea anemones, the team speculates.
Three sea spider species — C. tasmanica, C. Minor and another without bioluminescence — also fluoresced in green when Mallefet shone ultraviolet and blue light on them. Several amphibians and even platypuses are also fluorescent, glowing under certain wavelengths of light.
Mallefet isn’t sure why sea spiders fluoresce, but speculates the bioluminescence could be to attract mates. Or, since the light is visible only in the appendages, they might use it to see prey on the seafloor and, once zeroed in, collapse onto their victims, using a needlelike appendage in their proboscis to liquefy and suck up tissue. But this kind of scientific enlightenment will require taking imaging to the next level, with deep-sea video.

South African police have confirmed the death of a jogger, who went missing during a routine run last week, sparking a nationwide appeal for help finding her.
The body of Elizabeth Moselakgomo was identified by her relatives on Monday after it was discovered east of Johannesburg on Saturday. She is one of five women whose bodies have been found half-naked and bruised in the same area, Kempton Park.
Police said they were not linking the deaths to a serial killer but added that the "similarities are sufficiently concerningâ¦ to issue a public warning".
A jogger who knew Moselakgomo through their running club told the BBC the discovery of the five bodies was "very scary".
"It's sad to know that every woman in South Africaâ¦ can't just go outside. You can't just go to the shop and buy flowersâ¦ because you are always in danger," said Keamo Sefularo.
Police have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".
South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women.
Moselakgomo's body was found on Saturday night, badly bruised and partially clothed.
Just hours earlier on Monday, another woman's half-naked body was found about 25km (15 miles) away.
The latest discovery was made by a passer-by, who spotted the body on his way to work, police spokesperson Brig Athlenda Mathe told reporters at the scene.
One arrest has been made in connection with the discovery of the first body. The person is still in police custody.
The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders but these grim discoveries and Moselakgomo's death have sparked renewed outrage and fear among South Africans.
Tributes poured in for the avid runner, affectionately known as "Tsontso" after police confirmed her death. South Africans also shared the fear and anxiety women often feel in the country.
Lesedi Ledwaba, in a post on X, said: "Women are not free if we have to calculate where, when and with whom we can walk, run or exist safely".
This was echoed by Sefularo, who said Moselakgomo's disappearance had been "heavy for the club".
The 29-year-old also asked whether Moselakgomo would "still be here if maybe she had a small community to run with [or] one or three people"?
"As we always say, when we go out for runs, there's safety in numbers," she reflected.
Sefularo shared the measures she often took to keep safe while running, including avoiding taking the same route each day and making sure she ran in areas with good visibility.
Advocacy group Women for Change said the discovery of these bodies was angering.
"What is the purpose of having a protective service like the police if we have to make sureâ¦ we are [protecting] ourselves," the group's Merlize Jogiat asked.
Jogiat mostly blamed poor implementation of laws passed for the failure to curb the issue and said "pressure in numbers" from citizens could be the solution.
Moselakgomo's family thanked the public for the support in searching for the mother of one and commended her eight-year-old daughter for raising the alarm about her disappearance.
Authorities are yet to identify the remaining bodies.

US military has ‘on-orbit’ space weapons, Air Force Secretary reveals
Experts said the acknowledgment may lead to overt action by China, Russia.
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Air Force Secretary Troy Meink acknowledged that the U.S. has space weapons, a public revelation that some experts said could accelerate an arms race in orbit.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Mink said during his Monday morning speech at the Air, Space, Cyber conference here. “This is why the United States now has, on orbit, space-control weapons, capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversaries.”
Top service officials have typically been cagey when asked about U.S. space weapons, often citing national-security concerns. It also marks a major change in rhetoric. John Raymond, the service’s first chief of space operations, proclaimed in 2022 that “our primary purpose is to deter war.”
Defense experts were shocked by Meink’s admission on Monday morning, and said it will likely push the U.S. military’s main adversaries in space to acknowledge their capabilities, too.
“Well, that's huge, because I don't think any US government official has ever said that before,” said Victoria Samson, the Secure World Foundation's chief director of space security and stability. “The US also now has to accept the Chinese and Russians doing/saying the same. I don't think that this is going to be in the interest of US national security.”
Meink did not provide additional details on what type of on-orbit weapons the U.S. possesses.
Kinetic weapons, such as missiles, can create debris by destroying a target. Numerous top military officials have warned against using such weapons.
“Our commitment to responsible space operations is fundamental to our mission assurance and our role as stewards of the space environment,” Maj. Gen. Chris Povak, deputy director of the National Reconnaissance Office, said earlier this year.
Samson said that narrows her guess about what Meink was talking about.
“I'm going to guess what he's talking about is not a kinetic space-control weapon due to multiple comments government officials have said about avoiding debris causing counter space,” she said. “So I'm going to go with my first guess: space-based jammers, electronic warfare.”
Meink also made several other space-related announcements in his speech. The Air Force secretary said prototypes for the space-based Airborne Moving Target Indicator satellite constellation will be launched this month.
Meink also said that space-based interceptors, the cornerstone technology of President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense system, are now “flight ready.”
Last month, Space Force Gen. Michael Guetlein, Golden Dome’s direct-reporting program manager, warned that the missile defense project would be in dire straits if Congress can’t prioritize additional funding for the effort. The four-star general also said that initial development on space-based interceptors is underway and that the service has executed two “phenomenally successful” tests.
“All of the providers that are part of the competition are progressing exceptionally well,” Guetlein told reporters at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium.
“As everybody knows, there have been many who are developing capabilities to take those away from us, to threaten those things,” Meink said. “So, it is critically important that we maintain our dominance not only in the air but in space, and so that we've had to take steps to make sure that when we're threatened, we can take care of that.”

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is betting he can make billions flow north. About 300 CEOs and senior executives from some of the world's biggest investment firms will descend on the Four Seasons in Yorkville, a tony Toronto enclave of high-end restaurants and designer boutiques, for Carney's Canada Investment Summit this week. WATCH: Canadian tariffs on U.S. goods take effect, marking turning point in relations The investors collectively manage more than $120 trillion in assets, underscoring the scale of capital Carney hopes to tap as Canada tries to attract billions in new investment and reduce its economic dependence on the United States. "Canada is about so much more than being next to the United States," Carney said at a news conference last week in Banff, Alberta. "We have what the world wants." Carney pointed to Canada's vast energy and critical-mineral resources, its highly educated workforce and trade agreements that give businesses based in Canada access to roughly 1.5 billion consumers around the world. He said the turnout showed investors were interested in Canada on its own merits. "They are coming because of Canada," he said. "If they wanted to go to the United States, they would go to the United States." Few people know this crowd better than Carney. He ran the central banks of Canada and England, spent 13 years at Goldman Sachs and later chaired the boards of Bloomberg L.P. and Brookfield Asset Management, putting him very much in his element among the global investors and money managers gathering at the Four Seasons. Carney will court that capital Monday in separate meetings with the CEOs of Sydney-based Macquarie Group, whose asset-management arm is the world's largest infrastructure investment manager, and Singapore state-owned Temasek Holdings, a major global investment company. Washington then raised the stakes again, announcing bans on some Canadian imports and moving to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term U.S. government contracts. Trump's tariffs and efforts to shift manufacturing south of the border are undermining what was long one of the country's biggest attractions to foreign investors: reliable access to the enormous U.S. market under continental free trade. Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has launched Africa's largest ever share sale, offering a stake in his oil refinery to the general public in a deal that could raise as much as $2.1bn (Â£1.6bn).
The initial public offering (IPO) is for roughly 3% of the Dangote refinery, with the billionaire saying he wanted to give ordinary Nigerians the chance to share in the plant's success.
The refinery, which started production in 2024, is one of the largest in the world and took more than a decade to complete.
It now supplies more than 70% of Nigeria's energy consumption, and many Nigerians have expressed excitement at the prospect of owning a part of it.
Among them is Isah Salisu, who told the BBC he withdrew 50,000 naira (Â£28; $37) from his savings to invest.
"My hope is that my small money will one day grow big. I don't want to miss out as many I know are also investing," he said.
The IPO lasts for a month and the minimum purchase is 10 shares, costing about $4.
Economy and business expert Dr Abdulrazak Ibrahim Fagge told the BBC that Monday's event was historic.
But he warned investors that the price of the shares could fall, meaning people could lose some of their money.
"What prospective buyers, especially first-time buyers, should know is that they shouldn't invest all their money or money they would need in a couple of months," he said.
"They should invest something they could do without for the next three, four, five years."
He also warned people to be wary of scammers, saying there are people who would want to take advantage of those without good knowledge of the process.
"I will advise people to only deal with the institutions that have been listed," he said.
Nigeria is Africa's biggest oil producer but until the refinery was opened, most of the country's fuel had to be imported because of a lack of refining capacity in the country.
Born in Kano, Dangote, 67, has a net worth of around $28bn, according to Forbes magazine.
He made his fortune in cement and sugar in Nigeria before expanding to 16 other African countries.
His company Dangote Cement is Africa's largest cement producer.
The Lagos refinery was first announced in 2013 with an initial estimated cost of around $19bn, but construction did not begin until 2017. It was further delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic.
The site, in the Lekki Free Zone near Lagos, required massive land reclamation, with 65 million cubic metres of sand moved.
The refinery has a processing capacity of 650,000 barrels per day, making it the seventh-largest in the world.
The money raised by the share offer is intended to help double its capacity.

Here's what to know World Sep 14, 2026 12:20 PM EDT DOONBEG, Ireland (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump doubled down Sunday on his support for a united Ireland, saying it makes sense to merge the Republic of Ireland with the United Kingdom's Northern Ireland. "It just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland, and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is put them together," Trump said as he attended the Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg, western Ireland. READ MORE: Trump touches a nerve while in Ireland by saying reunification would be 'fantastic' It's not that simple. Trump's statement Saturday that Irish unification would be "fantastic" touched a live rail in the histories of Britain and Ireland that lies behind a century of division and decades of violence. Reaction, for and against, was swift. Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin urged politicians to "keep a calm perspective" on Trump's comments, and called some of the responses an overreaction. Northern Ireland's status has been divisive for a century When Ireland won independence from Britain a century ago and became a self-governing Roman Catholic-majority country, a six-county region in the north, which then had a Protestant majority, remained part of the United Kingdom. Northern Ireland was split between two main communities: nationalists — most of them Catholic — who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British. In the late 1960s, tensions exploded into "The Troubles," three decades of violence involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops left some 3,600 people dead in bombings, shootings and other attacks. A 1998 peace accord that the U.S. was instrumental in striking largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland's ultimate status unresolved by allowing people to identify as Irish, British or both. The Good Friday Agreement allows for a vote on unification if polls indicate it would likely pass, a threshold the U.K. government says has not been met. Ireland would also have to approve the change in a referendum. Peace in Northern Ireland has largely endured, but divisions remain deep over the conflict's legacy and the region's competing identities. Despite Trump's view, the issue of whether Northern Ireland's future lies with the U.K. or Ireland remains unresolved. The UK sought to downplay the remarks Trump said Sunday that his comments were "only my opinion," but also that he'd had "so much support." The British government sought to downplay them. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's office pointed back to his statement last week that he was "100%" behind the Good Friday accord and that the U.K. would only consider allowing a referendum "when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered." Opposition U.K. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said Trump was "shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state. This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension." Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump's remarks also were criticized by pro-British unionist politicians in Northern Ireland. Gavin Robinson, leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, posted on X that "Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington. Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people." Irish nationalists welcomed Trump's intervention Trump's remarks were striking because previous U.S. presidents – even those with Irish roots, like Joe Biden – have avoided commenting directly on the subject of unification. Sinn Fein, a political party that seeks unification and was allied during the Troubles with the Irish Republican Army, said it approved of Trump's comments, although the left-leaning party has little in common with him politically. Gerry Adams, who was Sinn Fein leader when the Good Friday accord was signed, said the "remarks by President Trump on the issue of Irish unity are welcome, even though we profoundly differ with him on many other matters." All the main Irish political parties support unification on paper, but Sinn Fein says Martin's centrist Irish government has failed to prepare for it to happen. Martin called some of the response to Trump's comments "an overreaction," noting the president had previously asked whether there would be a "merger" between Ireland and Northern Ireland. "It shouldn't be a surprise. He takes a different sort of perspective on things, we know that," Martin said Sunday. "I believe in Irish unity," he added. "Many political parties in the Republic believe in our unity. But we also of course believe in the Good Friday Agreement." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 303f5598226c.text: New York City and five other Democratic-led local governments sued the Department of Homeland Security to block a new Trump administration rule they say will drive immigrants and mixed-status families away from public benefits they can legally receive. Why it matters: The cities warn the rule could drive hundreds of thousands out of health, food and housing programs , worsening public health , increasing homelessness and shifting millions of dollars in costs to local hospitals and governments. What they're saying: "The federal government has waged a campaign of violence and terror," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a Monday news conference. "People could die as a result of these changes," he said. "… The data is clear: denying people services does not erase their need; it compounds it, generating a greater cost to our system that will be placed on the backs of working people for years to come. Nothing about this rule will reduce waste or keep Americans safer or improve New Yorkers' lives. It is simply a vehicle for confusion and a vehicle for cruelty." The White House and DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: The administration's rule takes effect this week and gives immigration officers broader discretion to deny green cards and visas based on immigrants' use of public benefits. Plaintiffs say the change abandons a century-old standard that limited who was considered a "public charge" to people who are "primarily dependent" on government cash assistance. The cities and counties argue the new rule will deter immigrant families from using Medicaid, SNAP, and housing assistance programs. New York City, Chicago, San Francisco and Seattle, along with Santa Clara County, California, and King County, Washington, filed the suit. Zoom in: DHS estimates over 950,000 people might disenroll or decline to enroll in public benefits, though the plaintiffs allege that estimate probably understates the effect. The final rule could potentially cause U.S. citizen family members to withdraw from benefit programs. Worth noting: The plaintiffs also say that the policy alert should have gone through a formal notice and comment because, despite being labeled guidance, it functions as a binding substantive rule. The rule follows a Republican reconciliation package in 2025 that limited legal immigrants' access to health insurance. The bottom line: The cities and counties argue the new rule gives immigration officers too much discretion, punishes lawful benefit use and will discourage potentially millions of people — including U.S. citizen children — from seeking food, health, housing and education assistance. 92edc75de416.text: A second federal judge blocked the U.S. Postal Service's new mail-ballot rules for the Nov. 3 midterms as the Supreme Court weighs whether to allow the restrictions in another case. Why it matters: Sunday's order adds another hurdle to the Trump administration's bid to upend mail voting . The blocked rules would allow the USPS to refuse ballots that don't clear new standards, with mail voting already underway in some states. The latest: U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee in Washington, D.C., concluded Congress empowered the Postal Service to move mail, not to force states to enroll mail voters in a federal portal or to refuse ballots that fail its checks. Nichols' ruling follows a similar order from U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston blocking parts of the same rule. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals left Talwani's injunction in place on Sept. 10. Talwani's order found the postal rules violate the U.S. Constitution and federal statute, while Nichols' new ruling relied entirely on his finding that Congress' Postal Reorganization Act doesn't allow many of the new rules. The White House and USPS did not immediately return requests for comment. Catch up quick: President Trump has long attacked mail voting, despite repeatedly using the method himself, including in August's Florida primaries . His March executive order directed the Postal Service to develop new envelope, tracking and voter-list requirements for mail voting. The Supreme Court already lifted an earlier injunction because the final rule hadn't been published yet. But after its publication, challengers returned to court and won new injunctions in Boston and D.C. The Trump administration is now asking the high court to stop Talwani's order and allow the new rules. Between the lines: Nichols said USPS might have the authority to issue rules on ballot-envelope designs, but he blocked the whole rule, finding its design, portal and rejection provisions too intertwined. Friction point: Even with enforcement blocked, voluntary preparations have exposed how exacting the new system could be. USPS initially rejected envelope designs from Florida's Leon County, a heavily Democratic area that includes Tallahassee, because the words "Return Service Requested" were 0.014 inches too close to other text, according to the Tallahassee Democrat. An anonymous USPS whistleblower also told Congress the Postal Service's portal was rushed, and a single scanning error could cause a batch of ballots to be rejected. The bottom line: The Supreme Court could rule on Talwani's injunction at any time. But Nichols' order now gives the administration a second injunction to overcome before it can enforce its mail ballot rules.
